newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: U.S. envoy seeks to defuse EU ire on Cuba sanction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy seeks to defuse EU ire on Cuba sanction.

text.p: The U.S. envoy charged with defusing anger over U.S. sanctions against Cuba pleaded with the European Union on Thursday not to take the matter to the World Trade Organisation. Stuart Eizenstat, President Bill Clinton's special envoy on the dispute, said that if the EU took the dispute to the World Trade Organisation it would erode public support for efforts to free world trade and strengthen the protectionists' hands. Eizenstat was speaking after a meeting with Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, whose country is current EU president and which enjoys close ties with the United States. "I made a very strong plea that this not be brought before a WTO panel because it as an inappropriate case for the WTO," Eizenstat told Reuters in an interview.

He said there had been "no meeting of minds" on Washington's Cuba sanctions, known as the Helms-Burton Act but was encouraged by Spring's pledge to try to resolve the dispute amicably while keeping pressure on Havana to democratise. "He (Spring) restated the strong objection the EU and its member states have to Helms-Burton. That objection was registered and understood."
"He said it was a goal of the Irish presidency to try to manage differences over Helms-Burton in a way that would maintain the strength of the EU-U.S. relationship."
Eizenstat said that if the issue was not brought to the WTO, "it would help defuse trade tensions and avoid a cycle of retaliation and counter-retaliation."
"It would only strengthen the hand of those in the United States who oppose the WTO as well as NAFTA (the North American Free Trade Agreement) and the whole multilateral system."

The EU has not yet made up its mind whether to take its objections to Washington's latest sanctions against Cuba to the World Trade Organisation, which oversees efforts to free world commerce and end protectionism.

The Helms-Burton Act was passed in July and will allow American citizens to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies that have benefitted from investments made in property confiscated by Havana since the Cuban revolution of 1959. "It only deals with that limited universe of companies who are using confiscated U.S. property and who have made additional investments on that property since the effective date of that law, March 12," Eizenstat said.
He said Spring was encouraged by the fact that Clinton has suspended for six months any enactment of the legislation, a step which has cut short any immediate EU recourse to the WTO.
Eizenstat argued that bringing democracy to countries under "totalitarian regimes" had been a shared EU-U.S. goal for decades in countries as far apart as Haiti and South Africa.
"We have worked as partners with Europe for 50 years spending hundreds of billions of dollars to protect and promote democracy on this continent," he said.
"There is no reason why Cuba, quite apart from Helms-Burton, ought not to be among those in which we work," he said.
Washington, he argued, was working with Europe now to bring peace and democracy to Bosnia and was at pains to understand why similar efforts in Cuba were causing such anger.
He was speaking at the end of a visit to Brussels and Bonn to try to defuse the dispute. He returned to Washington on Thursday and will visit Madrid, Bonn and London later.
